questions.prompt: An exam reading question asks: "What is the main idea of the text?" What should you look for?

options.text: One small detail, such as a name or a number.
Your own opinion about the topic of the text.
The whole message the writer wants to give.
The longest sentence you can find in the text.

questions.explanation: The main idea is the one message of the whole text: every paragraph supports it. A name or a number is only a detail, your own opinion is not in the text, and the length of a sentence says nothing about its importance.

questions.prompt:
The text says: "Leila joined the school choir in October because she loves singing."

Statement: "Leila joined the choir because her friends asked her to."

What is the right answer?

options.text: True — Leila joined the school choir.
False — she joined because she loves singing.
True — friends often ask us to join clubs.
False — Leila joined the school drama club instead.

questions.explanation: The choir is right but the reason is wrong, and one wrong part makes the whole statement false; the proof is the quotation "because she loves singing". "Leila joined the school choir" ignores the wrong reason, what friends often do is an opinion, not the text, and no drama club is mentioned.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence:

"My sister loves animals, so she wants to become a vet."

In this sentence, who does the word "she" refer to?
questions.explanation: A reference word must match its noun in number, kind and meaning. "She" is one female person, and the one who wants to become a vet is "my sister". The vet is what she wants to become, the animals are plural (they), and the writer would be "I".

questions.prompt:
Choose the correct verb form:

"Yesterday, the students ______ a documentary about the desert."
questions.explanation: The time marker "Yesterday" shows a finished action in the past, so the simple past is needed: "watched" (watch + ed). "watch" is the present simple, "are watching" the present progressive and "will watch" the future — none of them goes with "yesterday".

questions.prompt:
Choose the correct modal:

"You look tired. You ______ go to bed early tonight." (giving advice)
questions.explanation: Advice takes "should" (or "ought to") + the bare verb: "You should go to bed early." "mustn't" expresses prohibition — the opposite of what a tired person needs — "must" expresses obligation, too strong for friendly advice, and "might" expresses possibility.

questions.prompt:
Choose the correct verb form:

"The number of tourists in our region ______ since 2015." (increase)
questions.explanation: "Since 2015" links a moment in the past to now, so the present perfect is needed: has + past participle, "has increased" — it describes a change between the past and the present. "increased" needs a finished time such as "last year", and "is increasing" and "will increase" do not go with "since".

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about the benefits of reading?

options.text: My brother reads two comic books every week.
Yesterday I borrowed two books from our library.
That's why everyone should read a little every day.
Reading brings many benefits to young people.

questions.explanation: A topic sentence is general and announces the idea of the whole paragraph, as "Reading brings many benefits to young people" does. What my brother reads every week is one example, "Yesterday I borrowed…" is one personal event, and a sentence opening with "That's why" gives a result, so it closes a paragraph.

questions.prompt: You are on a crowded bus with a heavy bag. You want the young man next to you to help you, politely. What do you say?

options.text: Would you mind helping me with this bag, please?
Would you mind to help me with this bag, please?
You must help me with this bag.

questions.explanation: A polite request is "Would you mind + verb + ing?" (or "Could you + verb?"): "Would you mind helping me…?" After "mind" the verb takes -ing, so "to help" is wrong; "Mind this bag!" is a warning, and "You must…" expresses obligation — an order, not a polite request.
